newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Mutiny deals body blow to Afghanistan opposition.
newsitem.headline: Mutiny deals body blow to Afghanistan opposition.

text.p: The already shaky alliance battling Afghanistan's dominant Islamic Taleban has been dealt a body blow by the loss of at least one northern province after a key commander changed sides, according to reports.

The province of Faryab and the opposition-held half of its western neighbour Badghis fell to the purist Taleban on Monday when alliance commander General Abdul Malik switched sides and publicly announced his support for the Taleban, according to the reports.

The uprising spread to three other provinces. Reports from Faryab's provincial capital said that government buildings were flying the Taleban's trademark white flags and that a number of opposition fighters had been captured.
The front line in Badghis had remained static for more than 18 months until Monday and, despite frequent skirmishing, neither group had been able to break the lines until Malik's defection.
The Taleban control almost two thirds of Afghanistan, but they had made little strategically important headway since taking the capital Kabul last September.
The capture of Faryab will boost their confidence. Taleban-controlled Radio Shariat said on Monday night that they would pursue their foes.
"Our forces are advancing into Faryab province and we will chase down the defeated enemy," said the radio broadcast, monitored in Kabul.
The fall of the front line opens up the road to Mazar-i-Sharif 250 km (150 miles) to the east and the headquarters of General Abdul Rashid Dostum, the senior partner in the opposition alliance.

Reports from residents in Mazar-i-Sharif said Dostum's troops were still in command, but it is unclear if the opposition have managed to establish a new defensive line against the advancing Taleban and their new allies.
An opposition spokesman said on Monday that their first concern was to establish who was still loyal to the alliance.
"We don't know who is still loyal and who isn't, for us this is the most important thing." spokesman Dr. Abdullah told Reuters by satellite telephone on Monday night.
"We will be sending some reinforcements, people who originally came from Faryab," he added.
Dr. Abdullah said that he believed that Malik's action was tied to last week's killing of a commander, Abdur Rahman Haqqani, who he said was allied with Malik.
"Haqqani was one of them. His killing might have provoked this situation," Abdullah told Reuters by satellite telephone on Monday night.

However, many Afghan watchers tied the defection to the killing in still unexplained circumstances last year of Malik's brother Rasul Pahlivan, who was Dostum's strongest commander and a potential challenger for his power.
The opposition alliance includes Dostum, the forces of the government the Taleban ousted from Kabul last September, and a predominantly Shi'ite group based in central Afghanistan.
There has been friction between the different parties of the alliance, who fought each other before coming together in the face of the threat posed by the Taleban.

The Taleban, who emerged as a force in the country in late 1994, have vowed to take the whole of Afghanistan, disarm the factions whom they blame for the destruction that ensued after the fall of the communists, open the roads, and impose their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
